idiom_name: async/await over Task/Task<T> with IOCP-backed I/O
implementation_notes: The .NET platform absorbs the pattern: I/O-bound APIs return a Task or Task<T>, the runtime completes the underlying overlapped operation on an I/O completion port, and the async method's continuation resumes on a thread-pool thread (or on the captured SynchronizationContext). The compiler turns the async method into a state machine, so the completion handler is simply the code after await; the callback form survives only when wrapping APM (Begin/End) APIs with Task.Factory.FromAsync or when a high-throughput socket loop uses SocketAsyncEventArgs to avoid per-operation allocations.
pitfalls: Blocking on a task (.Result, .Wait()) can deadlock when a SynchronizationContext must run the continuation; await all the way instead.
async void is only for event handlers: exceptions escape to the synchronization context and callers cannot await or catch them.
Wrapping I/O-bound work in Task.Run only moves the wait to a pool thread; Task.Run is for CPU-bound work.
Starting unbounded concurrent operations with Task.WhenAll can exhaust sockets or connections; bound concurrency with a SemaphoreSlim.
